note.explanation: Proteins are polymers made from amino acids. Amino acids have a central carbon attached to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and an R group. The R group differs between amino acids. Proteins have many roles, including building structures, catalysing reactions, transporting oxygen and defending the body.
examples: Glycine has H as its side group.
Alanine has CH₃ as its side group.
note.simple: Proteins are like long chains made from amino-acid units. The different amino acids and their order help make different proteins with different jobs.

note.title: Proteins: building blocks and jobs
steps: Identify the amino acid units as the building blocks of proteins.
Remember that the R group varies between amino acids.
Link a protein to its function: for example, haemoglobin transports oxygen.
Use examples from the text to support your answer.
note.answer: Proteins are polymers of amino acids. Their functions include forming cell structures, catalysing biochemical reactions, regulating body processes, transporting oxygen, enabling muscle contraction, clotting blood and defending against pathogens.

mcqs.stem: Which part of an amino acid varies between different amino acids?
rationales: The amino group is a shared part of the general amino-acid structure.
The carboxyl group is a shared part of the general amino-acid structure.
The R group varies and gives different amino acids different side groups.
The central carbon atom is part of the general structure and is not the variable side group.

rationales: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised by our body and must be supplied by foods.
Essential amino acids are not defined as units found only in enzymes.

written.finalAnswer: Proteins form part of cell membranes and structures such as cartilage, hair and nails; enzymes catalyse biochemical reactions; some proteins act as hormones; haemoglobin transports oxygen; actin and myosin enable muscular contractions; fibrin causes blood clotting; and antibodies defend the body against harmful pathogens.

modelAnswer: Proteins are an important part of all cell membranes.
Some proteins, such as collagen and keratin, make almost whole structures of cartilage, hair and nails.
Enzymes are proteins that catalyse all biochemical reactions occurring in organisms.
Some proteins are hormones that regulate body processes.
Haemoglobin transports oxygen in the blood.
Actin and myosin are the main components of muscle cells and are responsible for muscular contractions.
Fibrin makes blood clot to prevent the loss of blood after an injury.
Antibodies defend the body against harmful pathogens.

Long questions may ask for the functions of proteins. State each function and pair it with the named protein example from your textbook.
For a question about essential and non-essential amino acids, distinguish them by whether our body can synthesise them.
Learn specific examples: haemoglobin transports oxygen, fibrin helps blood clot, and antibodies defend against pathogens.

explain.title: Proteins are made from amino acids
explain.body: Proteins are defined as the polymers of amino acids. Amino acids are the organic molecules that join in specific number and sequence to make proteins. Different proteins contain different numbers of amino acids: insulin has 51 and haemoglobin has 574.

explain.title: The amino-acid structure
explain.body: An amino acid is an organic molecule made of an amino group (NH₂), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen group (H) and a side group (R) which are attached to a central carbon atom. The R group varies: glycine has H, while alanine has CH₃.

explain.title: Essential and non-essential amino acids
explain.body: Essential amino acids: These are the 09 amino acids which cannot be synthesized by our body and are supplied by foods. Non-essential amino acids: These are 11 amino acids that can be synthesised in our bodies.

explain.title: Protein sources and functions
explain.body: Good sources include meat, fish, eggs, milk, pulses and beans. Proteins form cell membranes and body structures; enzymes catalyse biochemical reactions; some proteins act as hormones; haemoglobin transports oxygen; actin and myosin help muscular contractions; fibrin helps blood clot; and antibodies defend against pathogens.

mistakes: Do not confuse the R group with the amino group or carboxyl group; the R group is the variable side group.
Do not reverse the meanings of essential and non-essential amino acids: essential amino acids cannot be synthesised by our body.
Do not give a protein's name without its function in a long answer; connect haemoglobin with oxygen transport, fibrin with clotting and antibodies with defence.
Do not say that all proteins have the same number of amino acids; different proteins contain different numbers and sequences.
